The licence cannot be confirmed from the stated source. The Commons revision history shows that user Thue (a Copenhagen-based Wikimedian, not Adam Back) uploaded both 'Munitions T-shirt (front).jpg' and '(back).jpg' through UploadWizard on 2014-07-01, gave the author as 'Adam Back <adam@cypherspace.org>', and applied {{cc-zero}} with an empty permission field. There is no VRT ticket. The source page named in the upload, cypherspace.org/adam/rsa/uk-shirt.html, was re-fetched and its raw HTML read: it has no licence or public-domain statement. The shirt-design page (cypherspace.org/adam/shirt/design/) offers the artwork for people to print shirts but grants no licence either. The CC0 is therefore a third party's assertion for someone else's photograph, and the photographer is not named anywhere. Commons extmetadata does say 'CC0', so the rightsEvidence quoted in the record is accurate as far as it goes, but it is not independent evidence of a release.

The year and caption date '1997' are unsupported and probably wrong for the shirt. The upload gave the date as '1993-03-30'. On 2023-01-23 an anonymous IP changed it to '1997', inferring that 'the ruling that this code was 5D002 didn't happen until 1997 ... so this tshirt is after that'. That inference runs backwards. The shirt's own text says it is 'classified as a munition', and Adam Back's shirt homepage says the ITAR sections 120.17 and 121.1 (Category XIII) are 'the sections quoted on the shirt'. Encryption was controlled as a munition under the ITAR, not under the Commerce EAR's 5D002, until the December 1996 transfer. Back's media page states: 'Mockup of UK shirt appeared in the Japanese edition of Wired Nov 95.' The UK shirt therefore dates from 1995. The photograph itself is undated.

Checked OK otherwise: the local file opens as a 330x380 RGB JPEG, which matches thumbPx, and the thumbUrl returns HTTP 200. The alt text is accurate. The image shows a black shirt, worn, with 'WARNING This shirt is classified as a munition and may not be exported from the United States, or shown to a foreign national', 'RSA encryption in perl', lines of code and a large barcode in a white box. This matches Back's design page ('File warning.gz ... File rsa.gz ... Machine readable version of program: CODE128 barcode'). A UK-style wall socket is visible, which fits Back's alt text 'front of UK munitions T'.

Recommendation: keep the image only with the date corrected and the rights status marked unconfirmed (verified:false, which build-data renders as PENDING). If the project needs rights confirmed at the source, replace it with a better-documented image.

fieldFixes.caption: A UK-printed 'munitions' T-shirt (front), carrying RSA encryption in three lines of Perl as a protest against US export rules that classed encryption software as a munition. Adam Back's site says a mock-up of the UK shirt appeared in the Japanese edition of Wired in November 1995; the photograph itself is undated.

Caveat: the CC0 tag was applied by a third-party uploader (User:Thue, UploadWizard, 2014-07-01) with an empty permission field and no VRT ticket, and the cited source page carries no licence statement, so the release could not be confirmed at source. The Commons date '1997' was entered by an anonymous IP in 2023 as an inference; the upload had given '1993-03-30'.

issues: The correction goes too far in one place. It says the ''spy tool' purpose' is 'not supported by the record', but the record shows onion routing was meant partly to protect government, including intelligence, users. Syverson's paper (source 2) says: 'Law enforcement and intelligence agencies need to operate on the Internet without revealing their activities or intentions to those they are investigating or anyone else observing.' The 2004 Tor design paper (source 1) says: 'This work has been supported by ONR and DARPA.' The claim does say 'or the US military', and military funding is part of it. What the record does not support is an NSA origin or a surveillance purpose. The correction is reworded to concede the military and intelligence link while keeping the rebuttal of 'NSA' and 'surveillance tool'.

The three note quotes (1995 Goldschlag/Reed/Syverson at NRL; EFF funding in 2004; Tor Project, Inc. founded in 2006) are verbatim on the page. Source 1 (USENIX 2004 PDF) quote FOUND, and the affiliations (Dingledine and Mathewson 'The Free Haven Project', Syverson 'Naval Research Lab') are confirmed on the title page. Source 2 (Syverson 2011) quote FOUND. The correction's quoted phrase 'separate identification from routing' is in Syverson's abstract and section 1 ('We (David Goldschlag, Michael Reed, and I) began work on onion routing in late 1995 with the goal to separate identification from routing'). '1995–96' fits a late-1995 start and a first publication in May 1996 at Information Hiding.

fieldFixes.correction: Onion routing was invented in 1995–96 by David Goldschlag, Michael Reed and Paul Syverson at the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory (not the NSA) to 'separate identification from routing'. The military link is real. Syverson names law-enforcement and intelligence agencies that 'need to operate on the Internet without revealing their activities' among its intended users, and the 2004 Tor design paper says the work 'has been supported by ONR and DARPA'. But onion routing was built to hide its users' own traffic, not to watch anyone else's. Tor itself was designed in the early 2000s by Roger Dingledine and Nick Mathewson of the Free Haven Project, working with Syverson. Its code was released under a free-software licence when the network launched in 2002. The Electronic Frontier Foundation funded the work from 2004, and an independent nonprofit, the Tor Project, took it over in 2006. Navy origins and military funding are on the record. An NSA origin and a surveillance purpose are not.

fieldFixes.correction: The White House announced Clipper on 16 April 1993 as a 'voluntary program'. It was a government-designed chip for relatively inexpensive encryption devices that attach to an ordinary telephone. Each device had two keys, deposited separately in two escrow databases set up by the Attorney General and released only to officials with legal authority for a wiretap. The Attorney General promised to buy several thousand of the devices. In Matt Blaze's account, that purchase was the incentive for AT&T, which became the only company to build a full product around the chip. Industry and the public largely rejected Clipper, and critics feared that other encryption would eventually be outlawed. The scheme never became mandatory, and by the end of the decade the government had abandoned key escrow.
